title: Swimming: Science in the Water
summary: How science explains swimming: why water holds us up, how pushing water back moves us forward, why a long, flat body beats drag, how swimmers breathe, and how to stay safe.
poll: Every child should learn to swim, just like every child learns to read.

versions.title: Swim Smart
versions.text:
Jump in the pool. Splash! How do you swim? It is a bit of science.

First, you float. The water pushes up on you. Air in your chest helps, too. Take a deep breath. You will float best.

Next, you need to move. Push the water back with your hands. Kick with your feet. When you push the water back, you go the other way. You go forward!

Water is thick. It is much thicker than air. It slows you down. So swim flat and long, like a fish. Point your hands in front. Then you slide on.

Each way to swim is a stroke. There are four main strokes. The front crawl is the fastest.

You must breathe, too. Blow out bubbles in the water. Then turn your head and take in air.

Swimming is good for your heart. It makes you strong.

Learn to swim well. Swim with a grown-up near. Be safe in the pool and in the sea.

versions.title: Swim Smart
versions.text:
You jump into the pool. Splash! Now you swim from one end to the other. How do you do it? The answer is science.

First, you float. Water pushes up on your body. The air in your chest helps, too. If you take a deep breath, you float even better.

Next, you need to move. You push the water back with your hands and kick with your feet. When you push the water back, the water pushes you forward. That is how you move!

Water is thick. It is much thicker than air, so it slows you down. That is why good swimmers stay flat and long, like a fish. They point their hands in front of them so they can slide through the water.

Each way of swimming is called a stroke. There are four main strokes. The front crawl is the fastest one.

Swimmers must breathe, too. They blow out bubbles under the water. Then they turn their heads to take in air.

Swimming is good for your heart, and it makes many muscles strong.

Most of all, learn to swim well, and always swim with a grown-up nearby. Stay safe in the pool and at the beach.

Swimmers must breathe in a smart way. They blow out bubbles under the water, then turn their heads to take in air.

Swimming is good for your heart and makes many muscles strong.

Most important, learn to swim well, and always swim where a grown-up or lifeguard can see you. Stay safe in pools and at the beach.

versions.title: Swimming: Science in the Water
versions.text:
You dive into the pool with a splash and swim from one end to the other. It may feel natural, but every stroke depends on science.

First, your body has to float. Water pushes upward on any object placed in it. This upward push is called buoyancy. The air in your lungs makes you lighter, so if you take a deep breath and hold it, you will float higher in the water.

Next, you need to move forward. You push the water backward with your hands and kick with your feet. As you push the water back, the water pushes you forward with an equal force. Scientists describe this rule by saying that every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

Water is much thicker than air, so it slows you down as you move. This slowing force is called drag. To reduce it, skilled swimmers keep their bodies flat and long, like a fish. They stretch their arms in front of them in a straight line, a position called a streamline, so they can slide through the water.

Each style of swimming is called a stroke. There are four main strokes: front crawl, backstroke, breaststroke, and butterfly. The front crawl is the fastest, which is why most racers choose it.

Swimmers must also control their breathing. They blow out bubbles under the water and then turn or lift their heads to take in fresh air.

Swimming is excellent exercise, because it strengthens the heart and works many muscles at once.

Most important, learn to swim well, and always swim where an adult or lifeguard can watch you, whether you are in a pool or at the beach.

You dive into the pool with a splash and glide from one end to the other. Swimming may feel completely natural, but every movement you make in the water depends on scientific principles that engineers, coaches, and athletes study carefully.

First, your body has to float. When you enter the water, your body pushes some water aside, or displaces it, and the water pushes back upward with a force equal to the weight of the water displaced. This upward force is called buoyancy. The air in your lungs makes your body less dense, so if you take a deep breath and hold it, you will float noticeably higher.

Next, you need to propel yourself forward. You push the water backward with your hands and kick with your feet, and the water pushes you forward with an equal force. Scientists summarize this principle by stating that every action produces an equal and opposite reaction.

Water is about eight hundred times denser than air, so it creates considerable resistance as you travel through it. This slowing force is called drag. To minimize it, experienced swimmers keep their bodies flat and long, like a fish, and extend their arms forward in a position called a streamline. Many competitors also wear smooth caps and tight swimsuits for the same reason.

Each style of swimming is called a stroke. There are four main competitive strokes: front crawl, backstroke, breaststroke, and butterfly. The front crawl is generally the fastest and most efficient, which is why most racers choose it in freestyle events.

Swimmers must also regulate their breathing carefully, exhaling bubbles beneath the surface and then rotating or lifting their heads to inhale fresh air.

Swimming is excellent exercise, because it strengthens the heart and lungs and works numerous muscles simultaneously while placing little stress on the joints.

Above all, learn to swim confidently, and always swim where an adult or lifeguard can supervise you, whether you are in a pool or at the beach.

Because the air retained within your lungs renders your overall body noticeably less dense, inhaling deeply and deliberately holding your breath will consequently allow you to float measurably higher within the water.

Subsequently, you must actively propel yourself forward through the resisting medium. Competitive swimmers must additionally regulate their respiration with considerable care, exhaling bubbles methodically beneath the water's surface before subsequently rotating or elevating their heads to inhale fresh air without meaningfully disrupting their established swimming rhythm.

options: Float in one place without moving any part of the body at all
Breathe more often
Reduce drag so it is easier to move through the water
Make more bubbles
questions.why: A streamline keeps the body straight and long, which reduces drag.

wrong.A: A streamline is used while moving, not to stay still.
wrong.B: The position is not for breathing.
wrong.D: Bubbles come from breathing out, not from the streamline.

questions.stem: The article says drag is a "slowing force." Which object is most affected by drag?
options: A rock sitting still on the bottom of a pool
A swimmer moving quickly through the water
A towel lying on a chair beside the pool
A ball resting on the grass
questions.why: Drag acts on things moving through water or air, so a fast-moving swimmer feels it most.

wrong.A: A still rock is not moving, so drag does not slow it.
wrong.C: A towel on a chair is not moving through water.
wrong.D: A ball at rest is not moving through water or air.

questions.stem: How is the article mainly organized?
options: It tells a story about a famous swimmer's life
It compares swimming with running and cycling
It describes the events from one swimming race at the Olympics, in time order
It explains, step by step, the different science ideas behind swimming
questions.why: Each paragraph explains one idea: floating, moving forward, drag, strokes, breathing, and safety.

wrong.A: No famous swimmer's life is described.
wrong.B: Running and cycling are not compared.

questions.stem: The word "streamline" is made from "stream" and "line." How does this help explain its meaning?
options: The body forms a smooth, straight line that water can flow past
The swimmer must stay near a stream
The swimmer draws long, straight lines on the pool floor before each race
The body bends into a circle
questions.why: A stream flows smoothly, and a line is straight, so a streamline is a smooth, straight body shape.

wrong.B: The word describes a body position, not a place.
wrong.C: Nothing is drawn on the pool floor.
wrong.D: A streamline is straight, not curved.

MID.prompt: Imagine you are a swimming coach. Explain to a new swimmer how to float and how to move faster, using at least two key words from the article.
checklist: I explained how to float, using the article.
I explained how to move faster, using the article.
I used at least two key words correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: To float well, take a deep breath and hold it, because the air in your lungs creates buoyancy, the upward push of the water that helps keep your body near the surface. To move faster, push the water backward with your hands and feet, and keep your body flat and long in a streamline position so there is less drag slowing you down.

keyWords.definition: a force that works against something that is moving
keyWords.example: The cyclist felt strong wind resistance as she rode up the hill.

keyWords.definition: to push or drive something forward
keyWords.example: The rowers used long oars to propel the boat across the lake.

keyWords.definition: having a lot of matter packed into a small space; heavy for its size
keyWords.example: A stone is denser than a piece of wood, so it sinks.

keyWords.definition: working well without wasting time or energy
keyWords.example: An efficient runner keeps a steady pace and saves energy.

keyWords.definition: to push something out of its usual place
keyWords.example: When you climb into a full bathtub, your body will displace some water over the edge.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Swimming is mainly a matter of strength, and science plays little part.
Swimming relies on physical principles such as buoyancy, action and reaction, and drag, which swimmers use to move efficiently and safely.
Archimedes invented the four competitive strokes.
Swimsuits are the most important factor in a race, so a swimmer's training and body position matter much less.
questions.why: The article explains how buoyancy, equal and opposite forces, and drag shape every part of swimming.

wrong.A: The article argues the opposite: science explains every movement.
wrong.C: Archimedes described buoyancy; he did not invent strokes.

questions.stem: According to the article, how strong is the upward force of buoyancy?
options: It equals the weight of the water the body displaces
It is always twice a swimmer's weight
It depends only on how fast and how hard the swimmer kicks
It is the same as the force of drag
questions.why: The article says water pushes upward with a force equal to the weight of the water displaced.

wrong.B: The article gives no such rule.
wrong.C: Kicking is for moving forward, not for buoyancy.
wrong.D: Drag is a different force that slows forward motion.

questions.stem: About how much denser than air is water, according to the article?
options: Twice as dense
Ten times denser
About 800 times denser
Exactly as dense
questions.why: The article states that water is about eight hundred times denser than air.

wrong.A: This number is far too small.
wrong.B: This number is also too small.
wrong.D: Water and air are very different in density.

questions.stem: Why do many competitors wear smooth caps and tight-fitting swimsuits?
options: To stay warm in cold water
To float higher in the water without needing to breathe as often
To make the water less dense
To reduce drag, just as a streamlined body position does
questions.why: The article says competitors wear smooth caps and tight swimsuits for the same reason they hold a streamline: to minimize drag.

wrong.A: The article does not mention warmth.
wrong.B: Floating is linked to the air in the lungs, not swimsuits.
wrong.C: Clothing cannot change the density of water.

questions.stem: A swimmer breathes out all her air and stops moving. Based on the article, what will most likely happen?
options: She will float higher than before
She will sink lower, because her body is now denser
She will move forward quickly
Drag will push her upward
questions.why: The article explains that air in the lungs makes the body less dense; without it, she will float lower.

wrong.A: Breathing in, not out, helps a swimmer float higher.
wrong.C: Without pushing on the water, she will not move forward.
wrong.D: Drag slows motion; it does not push swimmers upward.

questions.stem: How is the force that propels a swimmer different from drag?
options: Both forces push the swimmer forward
The propelling force slows the swimmer down, while drag speeds her up through the water
The propelling force moves the swimmer forward, while drag works against that motion
Neither force exists in water
questions.why: The swimmer is propelled forward by the water's reaction to her push, while drag is resistance that slows her.

wrong.A: Drag slows the swimmer; it does not push her forward.
wrong.D: The article explains that both forces act in water.

questions.stem: The article calls the front crawl the most "efficient" stroke. What does this suggest?
options: It needs no breathing at all
It is the easiest stroke for beginners to learn on their first day in the pool
It is used only in the backstroke race
It produces a lot of speed for the energy used
questions.why: Efficient means working well without wasting energy, so the front crawl turns effort into speed well.

wrong.B: The article does not say it is easiest for beginners.
wrong.C: The front crawl is chosen in freestyle events, not the backstroke.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention Archimedes?
options: To show that the idea of buoyancy has been understood for a very long time
To argue that ancient Greeks were the best swimmers
To explain how pools were built in ancient times
To compare Archimedes with modern coaches and argue about which of them knows more about swimming
questions.why: Naming the ancient scientist who first described buoyancy shows that this principle has been known for centuries.

wrong.B: The article does not discuss ancient swimmers.

HIGH.prompt: Choose two scientific principles from the article and explain how a swimmer could use each one to swim faster or more safely.
checklist: I explained two scientific principles accurately.
I showed how a swimmer could use each one, with evidence from the article.
I used precise vocabulary, including at least two key words.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Two scientific principles explained in the article are buoyancy and drag, often felt as resistance in the water. Buoyancy is the upward push of water on an object, so a swimmer who takes a deep breath fills their lungs with air and floats higher, which helps them stay safe and conserve energy. Drag, however, slows a swimmer down because water is much denser than air, so skilled swimmers keep their bodies flat and stretch into a streamlined position to propel themselves through the water more efficiently. Understanding both principles helps a swimmer move faster while staying safe in the pool.
